front.title: Month 1
front.subtitle: The Beginning
front.baby: Conception happens around week 2, and about a week later the tiny ball of cells settles into the lining of your womb. The cells that will become the placenta begin reaching toward your blood supply.
front.you: You may not know yet. Hormones shift at implantation, and a missed period around week 4 is often the first sign. Some notice fatigue, tender breasts, or light spotting.
front.circle: Let the people close to you ease your load and meet your news with care. Your rest is her first world.
know: HER WORLD
In the pre- and perinatal view, her experience begins at conception, often before anyone knows she is there.
IMPRINTS
The circumstances of conception, and whether she was hoped for.
IF IT FEELS HARD
If you have known loss or a long road to conceive, hope and fear can arrive together. Both are welcome.

practices.name: Grounding
steps: Sit or stand, and feel your feet on the floor or your weight in the chair.
Notice the place where your body is most supported.
Breathe in slowly, and let the out-breath be a little longer.
Stay for three breaths. As you slow down, so does her world.
Return to this whenever you feel rushed or unsettled.

practices.name: Oxytocin moments
steps: A few times a day, do something you enjoy on purpose: a warm drink, sunlight, a hug, music.
Let yourself feel the pleasure for a full minute.
After a stressful moment, this helps wire her to move from stress back to calm.

healing.label: FOR YOUR OWN HEALING · YOUR OWN BEGINNING
steps: Reflect on what you know about how you came to be.
If you can, ask your mother or family how the news of you was received.
Write down what you learn, and what you feel as you hear it.
Invite your partner to explore their own beginning too.
healing.note: Meet whatever you find with kindness, for yourself and for those who came before you.

question: Am I wanted?
why: Her life begins with how she was conceived and hoped for.

front.title: Month 2
front.subtitle: The Discovery
front.baby: Her heart begins to beat around week 6. The start of her brain and spinal cord closes, arm and leg buds appear, and by week 8 every major organ has begun. The first touch receptors form around her mouth.
front.you: Nausea, deep fatigue, and a sharper sense of smell often peak now. For many this is the month of discovery, and joy, shock, fear, and ambivalence can arrive together.
front.circle: Ask for help through the nausea and fatigue, and let the people around you welcome her with you.
know: HER WORLD
She senses your emotions through your body's chemistry. Everyday stress is buffered, and each return to calm helps.
IMPRINTS
How the news was first received. Conflict at home can reach her too.
IF IT FEELS HARD
Waiting for first scans is full of uncertainty. Hard feelings are natural and need no guilt.

practices.name: Tell her what is going on
steps: When you feel a strong emotion, pause and take a slow breath.
Place a hand on your belly.
Name it simply: "I am tired and worried today."
Add: "This is about me, not you. You are welcome here."
This helps her know your feelings are yours, not hers to carry.

practices.name: Repair words for the news
steps: If the news was hard to take in, find a quiet moment, alone or with your partner.
Speak to her: "When we found out, we were scared. That was about us, not you."
Finish with: "We are so glad you are here."

healing.label: FOR YOUR OWN HEALING · WHAT SURFACES
steps: Notice if pregnancy brings up memories or feelings from your own childhood.
Write them down without judging them.
Meet them gently, the way you would meet a friend.
Invite your partner to notice what is surfacing for them too.
healing.note: If the feelings are big, reach out to a trauma-informed therapist. You do not have to hold them alone.

question: Am I welcome?
why: The news of her lands in your body, and she feels it.

front.title: Month 3
front.subtitle: Taking Root
front.baby: Now a fetus, she moves, stretches, hiccups, and swallows long before you can feel it. Sensitivity to touch spreads across her body, and some of your chemistry, including stress hormones, reaches her through the placenta.
front.you: Nausea often eases near the end of this month as the placenta takes over hormone production. First prenatal visits and screenings usually happen now, and many families begin sharing the news.
front.circle: Have someone with you at screenings and while you wait for results. A calmer home reaches her too.
know: HER WORLD
Nourishment, rest, and calm shape her lifelong health. Small, steady steps count.
IMPRINTS
Your own unresolved history may surface now. It deserves to be seen, gently.
YOUR CARE
Choose a model of care that fits you, and begin looking for a doula now, since many book early.

practices.name: A daily welcome
steps: Find a quiet moment each day this month.
Place a hand low on your belly, and take a slow breath.
Say hello: "Hello, little one. I know you are here."
Tell her one small thing about your day.
It is fine to begin before you feel ready. The welcome grows as you practice it.

practices.name: One steady step
steps: Choose one small change: a nourishing snack, an earlier night, a short walk.
Tell her about it: "This is for both of us."
After a week, notice how you feel, and choose the next step.

healing.label: FOR YOUR OWN HEALING · YOUR STORY, GENTLY SHARED
steps: If something from your past is surfacing, you do not have to carry it alone.
Share only what you choose, with someone safe: a partner, friend, or care provider.
Notice how it feels to be heard.
Remind yourself that healing now is a gift to you and to her.
healing.note: If it feels too big, ask your care provider for a referral to a therapist.

question: Is it safe to be here?
why: Your chemistry now reaches her through the placenta.

front.title: Month 4
front.subtitle: The First Flutters
front.baby: Her movements grow smoother and more coordinated, and she makes facial expressions. Her inner ear and taste buds are taking shape. Soon her movements will meet your hand.
front.you: Energy often returns, and your belly begins to show. Some mothers, especially those who have been pregnant before, feel the first flutters. Your sense of yourself begins to shift toward motherhood.
front.circle: Invite someone to notice her movements with you, and to shield you from frightening birth stories.
know: HER WORLD
Her movements are her way of telling her story. Noticing them is your first conversation.
IMPRINTS
Whether her movements are noticed and met.
STORIES YOU HEAR
Others may share fearful birth stories. You can choose what you take in.

practices.name: Hands on the belly
steps: Lie or sit comfortably, and rest both hands on your belly.
Breathe slowly and wait. There is no rush.
When you feel a flutter, say what you notice: "I feel you there."
Ask her simply, "How are you today?" and notice how she moves in answer.
Keep a small note of when she moves most. It becomes your shared rhythm.

practices.name: Choose your stories
steps: When someone begins a frightening birth story, you can say, "I would love to hear it after my baby is born."
Seek out two or three stories of births that went well.
If a story leaves you shaken, talk it through with someone you trust.

healing.label: FOR YOUR OWN HEALING · YOUR TIME IN THE WOMB
steps: Ask your mother what her pregnancy with you was like: calm, stressful, a time of loss or conflict.
Listen with compassion for her, too.
Notice how her story might live in you today.
Invite your partner to ask their mother the same.
healing.note: If your mother is not available, you can simply reflect and write what you imagine or sense.

question: When I reach out, will someone meet me?
why: Her movements are her first way of reaching out.

front.title: Month 5
front.subtitle: The First Sounds
front.baby: Hearing begins around weeks 18 to 20. Voices, music, laughter, and raised voices now reach her as vibration through the womb wall.
front.you: You will likely feel her move now. Your ligaments soften, and the anatomy scan usually happens around week 20. Feeling her move can turn an idea into a relationship.
front.circle: Let more loving voices reach her, and bring someone with you to the anatomy scan.
know: HER WORLD
Your voice, carried through your own body, is the loudest and clearest sound she hears.
IMPRINTS
The sound world of your home may stay with her. After a loud or tense moment, tell her what happened.
IF NEWS IS HARD
If the scan brings unexpected news, you can take time before deciding. Fear or grief is natural.

practices.name: The kick game
steps: Choose a time she is often active, such as after a meal or when you lie down to rest.
Rest your hand where you feel her move, and take a slow breath.
When she kicks, press gently back once in the same spot and say, "Hello, I feel you."
Wait and notice. If she answers, press again. If not, simply rest your hand there.
Invite your partner to try it, speaking close to your belly.

practices.name: A song for her
steps: Choose one song, rhyme, or short phrase that feels like yours.
Sing or say it to her once a day, at about the same time if you can.
After she is born, use the same one when she needs comfort. She may know it.

healing.label: FOR YOUR OWN HEALING · YOUR BIRTH STORY
steps: Ask your mother or family how you were born: how long the labor was, who was there, and whether you were kept close.
Write down what you learn, and what you feel as you hear it.
Notice anything that echoes your hopes or fears for this birth.
Share it with your partner, and invite them to explore theirs.
healing.note: If it stirs strong feelings, go gently, and reach out to someone you trust or a therapist.

question: Is my world a kind place?
why: Hearing begins, and the sounds of home reach her.

front.title: Month 6
front.subtitle: The Rhythm
front.baby: She begins to respond to sound, often startling at a sudden noise. Her lungs begin making surfactant and her brain grows quickly. She moves through loose cycles of rest and activity, at a rhythm much slower than yours.
front.you: Your belly grows quickly, and back aches, heartburn, or swelling may begin. A glucose screening is usually offered between weeks 24 and 28. Your thoughts may begin turning toward the birth.
front.circle: Ask for real rest, and let others take on tasks. The calm rhythm of your home is the world she feels.
know: HER WORLD
The pace of your days and your moments of settling may be how she learns rhythm.
IMPRINTS
Everyone brings a birth story into the birth room. Yours, and your mother's, may come to mind now.
IF NEWS IS HARD
A diagnosis such as gestational diabetes is information to guide your care, not a judgment on your body.

practices.name: Three daily oxytocin breaks
steps: Pick three daily cues, such as waking, lunch, and bedtime.
At each, take one minute for something pleasant: a stretch, a song, a warm hand on your belly.
Breathe slowly and let yourself enjoy it.
Practiced now, this groove of calm is easier to find in labor and after birth.

practices.name: Gather your support
steps: Choose a childbirth class that fits you, and check in on your doula.
Name the rest you need, and ask family or work for it in plain words.
Choose one person you can call on a hard day.

healing.label: FOR YOUR OWN HEALING · YOUR BELIEFS ABOUT BIRTH
steps: Write three words that come to mind when you think of birth.
For each, ask where it came from: your own birth, your mother, films, or friends.
Keep the words that strengthen you, and let the others soften.
Invite your partner to do the same, and share your words.
healing.note: A belief you can name is a belief you can choose to change.

question: Can I rest here?
why: Her first rhythms of rest take shape in the climate around her.

front.title: Month 7
front.subtitle: Light and Voices
front.baby: Her eyes open and can sense light through your belly. She gains fat, practices breathing, and spends much of each day in REM sleep, the stage linked with dreaming. The voices she hears most will be familiar after birth.
front.you: The third trimester begins. Sleep grows harder, breath shorter, and practice contractions more noticeable. Anticipation grows, and so can fear of birth.
front.circle: Choose people who hear your fears without adding to them, and help your partner ready their voice for her.
know: YOUR HORMONES
The hormones of birth flow best when you feel safe, private, and unobserved.
IMPRINTS
Fear in the room: yours, your family's, or a provider's past cases.
PLANS CAN CHANGE
Exploring other paths, such as a longer labor or a cesarean, lets you meet a change as a choice.

practices.name: Pacing
steps: Each day, choose one moment to slow everything down: walk, speak, and move at half speed.
Add small pauses between tasks: one breath, a hand on your belly.
Notice how she moves when you slow down.
Her rhythm is slower than yours. Slowing down helps her stay with you.

practices.name: Imagine your birth space
steps: Picture where you will give birth. What helps you feel safe there?
List what you want: dim light, music, who is there, freedom to move.
Choose who will speak up for you, such as your partner or a doula, and share the list.

healing.label: FOR YOUR OWN HEALING · FEARS AND THEIR ROOTS
steps: Write down your fears about this birth.
Beside each, ask: does it echo my own birth, my mother's, or a story I heard?
Naming where a fear comes from can soften its hold.
Invite your partner to speak their fears too, so they do not fill the birth room unspoken.
healing.note: Feeling fear is natural. Talking it through is how it loosens.

question: Can I trust those around me?
why: She knows the voices near her, and feels the fear or calm in them.

front.title: Month 8
front.subtitle: The Turning
front.baby: She gains weight quickly and space grows tight. Studies first show her responding to your voice differently from other voices. Antibodies cross the placenta, and many babies settle head down now.
front.you: Your uterus presses up under your ribs and builds oxytocin receptors for labor. Your breasts may begin leaking colostrum. Nesting energy often arrives.
front.circle: Plan help for after the birth, and keep your bond with your partner warm. She is held inside it.
know: POSITION
If she is still breech near 36 weeks, options include waiting, gentle positioning, a version, or a breech birth with a skilled provider.
IMPRINTS
Space and holding as room grows tight, and how decisions about her are made.
YOUR CHOICES
You can ask about benefits, risks, and alternatives, take a moment, and say yes or no.

practices.name: Tell her what you would like
steps: Sit or lie comfortably, and rest your hands on your belly.
Breathe until you feel settled.
Speak to her: "When you are ready, you can turn head down. That will make the way out easier."
Thank her, whatever she does.
Repeat a few times a week, gently, without pressure.

practices.name: Practice your questions
steps: For any choice, ask: What are the benefits? The risks? The alternatives? What if we wait?
Try it on a small choice at your next visit.
Remember you can always say, "I need a moment to think."

healing.label: FOR YOUR OWN HEALING · WITH YOUR PARTNER
steps: Partners carry fears and birth stories too.
Invite your partner to share how they imagine the birth, and what worries them.
Listen without fixing.
Agree on one way they can support you when it matters most.
healing.note: A partner who feels heard can hold the space more steadily for you both.

question: Will I be held as space grows tight?
why: Room grows tight, and she begins to feel the walls holding her.

front.title: Month 9
front.subtitle: Ripening
front.baby: Her lungs finish maturing, and full term arrives at 39 to 40 weeks. Research suggests her own lungs release a signal that helps start labor, so she may have a part in deciding when birth begins.
front.you: She may drop lower, easing your breath but adding pressure. Practice contractions grow stronger and your cervix begins to soften. You may feel ready, impatient, or afraid, sometimes all in one day.
front.circle: Let someone share the waiting and answer the questions, so you can turn inward and trust her timing.
know: TIMING
Labor usually begins when you are both ready. Induction is a choice to weigh, not an automatic step.
IMPRINTS
Being waited for, or hurried: whether her readiness is trusted.
SUPPORT
Plan who will stay with you through anything unexpected.

practices.name: Tell her about the birth to come
steps: Choose a calm moment each day, and rest a hand on your belly.
Tell her what will happen: "Soon you will be born. It will be big, and I will be with you."
Tell her who will be there to meet her.
Rehearse the first words you want her to hear: "You made it. I am so happy you are here."

practices.name: Gathering colostrum
steps: First ask your provider if it is right for you. It is usually begun after 37 weeks.
Once a day, with clean hands, gently massage, then press behind the areola.
Collect any drops in a small syringe and store them as your provider advises.

healing.label: FOR YOUR OWN HEALING · WAITING WITH KINDNESS
steps: When pressure to have the baby already builds, notice how it feels in your body.
Write: "What do I need while I wait?"
Ask for it, from your partner, family, or care team.
Remind yourself and her: "We will meet when we are both ready."
healing.note: Impatience, fear, and readiness can all arrive in one day. None of them needs guilt.

question: Will I be given time?
why: Her own body helps signal when she is ready to be born.

front.title: Labor
front.subtitle: The Threshold
front.baby: Each contraction presses and releases her whole body like a long embrace. Her own stress hormones surge to protect her and prepare her lungs. She may sense pressure, rhythm, and pause.
front.you: Oxytocin brings the waves, and endorphins ease pain and carry you inward. You labor best when you feel private, safe, and unobserved, free to move, eat, and drink.
front.circle: Have someone stay the whole way and guard a quiet space, telling her, too, what is happening.
know: THE SPACE
When labor feels watched or unsafe, adrenaline rises and can slow it. Dim light, quiet, and trusted people keep it flowing.
IMPRINTS
The journey through, supported or interrupted. Ask the reason for any procedure.
IF PLANS CHANGE
Pain is part of labor; suffering is not, and choosing relief needs no guilt. Ask for someone by your side, clear explanations, and time to respond.

practices.name: Tell her what is happening
steps: As a wave begins, rest a hand on your belly if you can.
Say, out loud or inside, "Here comes another wave. We are doing this together."
When it passes: "That one is over. You are doing well."
Before anything changes, such as moving, a monitor, or a transfer, tell her first.
When you cannot speak, your partner or doula can speak to her for you.

practices.name: Ground between waves
steps: Feel your feet, or the places your body is held: the bed, the ball, the water.
Breathe out a little longer than you breathe in. Let your jaw and shoulders soften.
Rest in the pause. She feels you settle, and the next wave can find you calmer.

healing.label: FOR YOUR OWN HEALING · BEFORE LABOR
steps: If you have given birth before, tell that story to someone who listens without judgment.
Notice which moments still feel heavy, and name what you would want to feel different this time.
Share those wishes with your partner and birth team, so they can help protect them.
healing.note: If an earlier birth was hard, support from a trauma-informed therapist can help before this one begins.

question: Can I make it through?
why: Labor presses her whole body, wave after wave.

front.title: Birth
front.subtitle: Through the Gate
front.baby: In the final push, a surge of noradrenaline makes her alert, often with wide open eyes at your first meeting. She takes her first breath, and her circulation changes course within minutes. Light, air, sound, and gravity arrive all at once.
front.you: A surge of adrenaline gives you strength for the final pushes, and many mothers feel a burst of energy to meet the baby. Pain medication can soften this surge, so you may both be less alert at first.
front.circle: Keep a familiar voice with you and with her, so neither of you is alone if plans change.
know: HER FIRST SENSES
Harsh lights, noise, and routine suctioning can overwhelm her. You can ask for dim light and calm.
GENTLE CARE
You can ask for delayed cord clamping, and for a gentle cesarean if surgery is needed.
IF IT CHANGES COURSE
A cesarean or separation is not a failure. She can be told what is happening and held close as soon as possible.

practices.name: Narrate her arrival
steps: As she arrives, slow everything down.
Say to her: "You are out now. You made it. You can take a breath."
Pause, and let her look at you.
Then: "I am so happy you are here. I love you."
If you cannot speak, your partner can say it for you.

practices.name: Repair after intensity
steps: If the birth was intense or plans changed, ground yourself: feel your body, take a breath.
Tell her: "That was a lot. It is over. You are safe now. It was not your fault."
Repairs build stronger trust than if the hard moment had never happened.

healing.label: FOR YOUR OWN HEALING · KINDNESS FOR YOURSELF
steps: Remind yourself that you made the best choices you could with what you knew in the moment.
Offer yourself the words you offered her: "That was a lot. You are safe now."
Let someone care for you, too.
healing.note: A birth that changed course is not a failure. You can meet yourself with the same kindness you offer her.

question: Is it safe to arrive?
why: Light, air, and sound meet her all at once.

front.title: First Hour
front.subtitle: The Welcome
front.baby: Placed skin to skin, she warms, steadies her heart and breathing, and may crawl toward the breast on her own. She knows your smell, your heartbeat, and your voice, now from the outside.
front.you: Skin to skin, oxytocin and prolactin peak. Oxytocin helps the placenta release and protects against bleeding, and prolactin begins milk and mothering. Awe, relief, and exhaustion may arrive together.
front.circle: Protect a quiet golden hour, so she is welcomed skin to skin, and by more than one person.
know: THE GOLDEN HOUR
You can ask for newborn checks to happen on your chest, and for the first bath to wait.
IMPRINTS
Welcome or separation. Staying together is part of gentle, humanistic care.
IF YOU WERE APART
The bond is not lost. Skin to skin and closeness can begin as soon as you are together.

practices.name: Skin to skin
steps: Ask that she be placed on your bare chest, with a warm blanket over you both.
Let her rest, breathe, and find her way.
Watch her cues: rooting, licking, moving toward the breast.
Keep the first hour quiet and unhurried. Visitors can wait.

practices.name: Tell her the story of her birth
steps: In the days after, hold her close and tell her the story of her birth, slowly.
Name what happened, and how it felt.
If anything was hard: "I am sorry that happened. It was not your fault. You are safe now."
End with: "I love you."

healing.label: FOR YOUR OWN HEALING · TELLING YOUR BIRTH STORY
steps: In the weeks after, tell the story of this birth to someone who listens without judgment.
Invite your partner to tell theirs too.
Offer the same kindness to the younger self in your own birth story.
Watch for lingering distress, such as flashbacks, numbness, or avoidance.
healing.note: If distress stays, reach out to perinatal mental health support. You can heal alongside your baby.

question: Do I belong here, with you?
why: Skin, smell, and voice tell her where she has arrived.
